status: Closed — invocation batching and spawn-failure reporting fixed; caller audit found no additional unbounded git-derived argv caller
finding: scripts/check-encoding-touched.ts built a single --files argument holding every touched text file and spawned the guard once. On a busy worktree that argument reaches tens of kilobytes and exceeds the Windows command-line ceiling, so process creation fails with ENAMETOOLONG, spawnSync returns status null with no stdout or stderr, and the script's fallback reported that as a bare exit 1. The failure mode is byte-identical to a genuine encoding violation: same exit code, no output either way. The guard therefore stopped guarding precisely when the tree was busiest, which is exactly the parallel-captain condition it exists for, and every caller that reads its exit code was silently misinformed.
expectedBehavior: The encoding guard must remain runnable regardless of how many files are touched, and must never terminate non-zero without naming why. Invocations must be batched against the shared platform argv budget rather than assembled unbounded, every touched file must still reach the guard exactly once, and a spawn that never ran must be distinguishable from a guard that found a violation.
evidenceOrRepro: Reproduced on 2026-08-28 at the repository root: 803 touched text files produced a joined --files argument of 61,895 characters against a Windows ceiling of 32,767. `node --strip-types scripts/check-encoding-touched.ts --mode touched` exited 1 with zero bytes on both stdout and stderr; a direct spawnSync of the same argument returns status null, signal null, error ENAMETOOLONG. After the repair the same command runs three batched invocations and reports a verdict for each. Note this is the same class of defect the Git pathspec callers already solved: packages/cli/src/commands/git-governance/implementation/pathspec-argv-batching.ts existed and owned the platform ceiling policy, but the encoding guard did not use it.
containment: Quickfix on 2026-08-28 (claude-008). The guard invocation is planned through planPathspecBatches with the guard's own fixed arguments charged to every batch, so there remains exactly one place that knows the platform ceiling. Because the guard joins paths with commas while the budget charges each path as a separate argument, every planned batch is strictly smaller than budgeted. A batch whose spawn returns a non-numeric status now prints the underlying errno and the batch size before contributing exit 1, and a single path too long to batch under any split is reported rather than silently truncated. Batch verdicts are aggregated so any failing batch fails the run. Regression in tests/cli/encoding-guard-argv-budget.test.ts asserts that one oversized argument is genuinely unspawnable on Windows, that batching preserves every file and keeps each invocation under budget, that every planned batch reaches the guard and passes on clean tracked sources, and that the script never terminates with empty output.
followUp: The explicitly observed `.atm-runtime-cache/` files are already covered by the repository's explicit `.gitignore` rule and are excluded from touched-file auto-discovery; their cleanup/encoding policy remains a separate hygiene decision, not a failure of this guard. A read-only caller audit on 2026-09-06 found no additional caller that assembles a repository-sized git-derived file list into argv without the shared budget policy. A future lint/contract test can enforce that invariant across new callers.
